envelope.text: use and dropped when done. Here a timer is an entry in the executor's STATIC

why:
our `Timer` is an entity in the executor's static table with a MODE (`inert`, `oneshot`, `repeating`) that can be changed in place, because a static table cannot grow a timer at runtime and re-arming is how a one-shot is reused. rclcpp's `WallTimer` is created per use and cancelled when done, which needs an allocation each time.

phase-428 W6 (2026-09-06) — disposition, required because this row's SHAPE CORRESPONDS: the name exists on the ported surface and the correlator files it `same`, so nothing in a build says the contract differs. That is the class RFC-0089 exists for.

UPSTREAM'S CONTRACT: `rclrs::Timer` is `Arc<TimerState>`, created per use and dropped when done. Note what is NOT a difference: upstream's `TimerState` also carries `set_inert` / `set_repeating` / `set_oneshot`, so the MODE vocabulary the text above describes is shared with rclrs rather than invented here.

OURS: an entity in the executor's static table whose mode is changed in place, because a static table cannot grow a timer at runtime.

HOW A USER FINDS OUT: the LIFETIME is what differs, and it shows at creation — there is no per-use construction to write, so a ported timer is declared in `register` and re-armed rather than re-created. Separately, four predicates differ in RETURN TYPE (`is_canceled`, `is_ready`, `time_since_last_call`, `time_until_next_call`: `Result<_, RclrsError>` upstream, bare values here). The correlator reports those as `same:ret` only since the phase-428 W6 `_ret_of` fix — before it, `_ret_of` was handed the flattened item instead of its `overloads` and always answered None, so the return-type comparison could not fire anywhere in the tree. Each of the four is its own row, verdict `extension`.

ADOPT-BOUNDED for the name and the mode vocabulary; the envelope is the lifetime.

issue 1637 (2026-10-05) — ENVELOPE WRITTEN where a porting user reads it. MEASURED what this key is: the correlator folds rclrs's `State` suffix, so `rust:Timer` is our `nros::TimerState` (`packages/core/nros-node/src/timer.rs`). Its rustdoc said only "Internal timer state / Stored in the node's timer collection"; it now states the lifetime bound (declared once in the static table, re-armed in place by `set_repeating`/`set_oneshot`/`set_inert`, not created per use).
